x: Punch-marked (Aahat) coins, mostly of silver, are the earliest coins found in India, dating from about the 7th–6th century BC to the Mauryan period. Kushana, Gupta and Sultanate coins came much later.
t: Recall the earliest coin type of India.

x: Option C is incorrect: Chandragupta I, not Chandragupta II, was the first Gupta ruler to issue coins. Chandragupta II's silver coins marked his victory over the Sakas, and Gupta gold coins were called Dinara.
t: Discriminate Chandragupta I from Chandragupta II.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Vima Kadphises was the first Kushana to issue gold coins, and he made gold coinage regular and large-scale.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Agathocles issued bilingual Greek and Brahmi coins, Kanishka showed the Buddha on his coins, the Yaudheyas showed Kartikeya with a peacock, and Iltutmish issued regular coinage from Delhi, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Link each ruler to the feature of his coins.

x: I and III are correct: Satavahana coins were of lead, copper, bronze, silver and potin, and potin was a mixture of copper, silver and lead. II is false because the Satavahanas issued no gold coins.
t: Recall which metals the Satavahanas did not use.

x: All four are correct: Gupta gold coins were Dinaras and silver coins Rupakas, the largest Gupta hoard was found at Bayana in Bharatpur, Rajasthan, and Chandragupta II's silver coins marked his victory over the Sakas.
t: Check each statement on Gupta coins separately.

x: Strato II, a late Indo-Greek ruler, is known for his lead coins. Most Indo-Greek coins were of silver, which is the trap.
t: Recall the metal of Strato II's coins.

x: A hoard of 16 coins of the Indo-Greek king Menander was found at Bairat in Rajasthan.
t: Recall the number of Menander coins at Bairat.

x: Both are true: Indo-Greek coins carry the name and portrait of the issuing king, so they are the first Indian coins attributable to individual rulers, and most of them were silver drachms.
t: Judge each statement separately on Indo-Greek coin features.
s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Indo-Greeks were the first rulers in India whose coins can be definitely attributed to particular kings.
Statement B: Indo-Greek coins were issued mostly in silver.

x: The Yaudheyas showed Kartikeya with a peacock, the Saka-Kshatrapas used a 1:35 gold-silver ratio, Chastana issued silver and rare copper coins, and Iltutmish set up regular coinage at Delhi, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Link each issuer to the feature of its coins.

x: All three are correct: Chandragupta I was the first Gupta to issue coins, and Chandragupta II, called Sakari, issued silver coins after defeating the Sakas.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Iltutmish's silver tanka weighed about 175 grains, and his copper jital became the small coin; together they formed the basic Sultanate currency.
t: Recall the standard weight of the Sultanate silver tanka in grains.
s: The silver tanka introduced by Iltutmish weighed about how much?

x: Muhammad Ghori issued gold coins showing the goddess Lakshmi, copying the earlier Gahadavala type. Kanishka and Chandragupta II were not Muslim rulers.
t: Recall which Muslim ruler copied Hindu coin designs.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Iltutmish received recognition from the Abbasid Caliph in 1229, and after that he put the Caliph's name on his coins.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Three are correct: Kushana gold coins circulated widely and regularly, Kushana copper coins were common, and lead was a major Satavahana metal. Statement IV is false because the Satavahanas issued no gold coins.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Kujula Kadphises, the first Kushana ruler, issued copper coins. Vima Kadphises later introduced gold coins on a large scale.
t: Discriminate Kujula Kadphises from Vima Kadphises.

x: Punch-marked coins were mostly of silver, though a few copper ones are known. Gold coins began only with the Indo-Greeks and Kushanas.
t: Recall the main metal of punch-marked coins.

x: Agathocles issued silver coins showing Sankarshana and Vasudeva, Chandragupta II issued silver Rupakas, Iltutmish issued silver and copper coins, and Muhammad Ghori's coins carried the Kalma, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Link each ruler to the feature of his coins.

x: I and III are correct: the Harappans used gold, silver and copper, and copper and bronze were their main working metals. II is false because iron was unknown to the Harappans.
t: Check each statement about Harappan metals.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Gold, silver and copper are included in Harappan metal evidence.
II. Iron was the principal metal found at Harappan sites.
III. Copper and bronze were associated with the Indus Valley Civilization.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Option C is incorrect: iron was not found at Harappan sites. Copper was the first metal used, the Rigvedic Aryans used gold, silver and copper, and the Indus people used copper and bronze.
t: Recall which metal the Harappans did not know.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: iron spread in North India during 1000–600 BC, and the Iron Age began in the Later Vedic period. R gives the start date, not the reason for the spread.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Kushana coins were mainly of gold and copper, Gupta coins of gold and silver, Kalachuri coins of gold, silver and copper, and Sher Shah's currency is known for the silver Rupiya and copper Daam, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Recall the metals used by each dynasty.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Kushana coins
(b) Gupta coins
(c) Kalachuri coins
(d) Sher Shah currency
List-II
(i) Gold and silver
(ii) Silver Rupiya and copper Daam
(iii) Gold and copper
(iv) Gold, silver and copper

x: Both are true: the Iron Age in India began in the Later Vedic period around 1000 BC, and the Indo-Greeks issued gold coins in the 2nd century BC.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Satavahana coins were of lead, copper, bronze, silver and potin. Options with gold are wrong, as the Satavahanas issued no gold coins.
t: Eliminate the options containing gold.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Sher Shah issued coins in pure gold, silver and copper, and his Rupiya held 173 grains of pure silver. R describes one coin, not the whole currency.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Sher Shah's copper Daam weighed 380 grains. 178 grains was the weight of the silver Rupiya, and 64 is the Rupiya–Daam ratio.
t: Discriminate the weights of the Rupiya and the Daam.

x: One Rupiya of Sher Shah was worth 64 copper Daams, a ratio of 1 : 64.
t: Recall the exchange rate of Rupiya and Daam.

x: Three included gold: Indo-Greek, Kushana and Gupta coins. Satavahana coins had no gold.
t: Check each coinage for gold.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Sher Shah's Rupiya weighed 178 grains in all, of which 173 grains were pure silver. The silver content does not cause the total weight.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Under the Guptas, Udrang was land revenue, Bhag the king's share of produce, Udakabhog the irrigation tax and Uparnika a tax on border-land farmers, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the meaning of each Gupta tax term.

x: Both are true: in the Gupta period Vishti, or forced labour, was counted as a form of tax, and tax-free land was granted to Brahmins and religious functionaries.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Alauddin Khalji was the first Sultan to measure cultivated land and fix revenue on that basis. Akbar's Zabt system came much later.
t: Recall who first measured land for revenue.

x: Diwan-i-Mustakharaj was the department Alauddin Khalji created to recover arrears of revenue from officials and collectors.
t: Recall the department for revenue arrears.

x: Option A is incorrect: Alauddin Khalji abolished, not expanded, the privileges of the Khuts, Muqaddams and Chaudharis. This weakened the intermediaries and let the state collect revenue more directly.
t: Check what happened to the intermediaries' privileges.

x: Alauddin reclaimed Milk and Waqf lands into Khalisa, fixed Kharaj at 50% of the yield, and levied Ghari as house tax and Charai as grazing tax on milch animals, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Recall the meaning of each Khalji tax term.

x: Maal was Mughal land revenue, Madad-i-Mash a revenue-free grant to learned and pious men, Shah Jahan's pilgrim tax was levied at Banaras and Allahabad, and Aurangzeb's Jizya fell on non-Muslims, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the meaning of each Mughal revenue term.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the pilgrim tax at Banaras and Allahabad was opposed because Kavindracharya and the Banaras pandits petitioned Shah Jahan to abolish it.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All four are correct: women, slaves, children below 14, and beggars and the unemployed were exempt from Aurangzeb's Jizya.
t: Check each exempt group separately.

x: Under Aurangzeb, Jizya was graded by income: 12 dirhams a year below 200 dirhams, 24 dirhams for 200–10,000, and 48 dirhams above 10,000.
t: Recall the Jizya rate for the lowest income group.

x: Both are true: Chauth (one-fourth) and Sardeshmukhi (one-tenth) were the main Maratha revenue claims on neighbouring territory.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: The Salt Tax was the main target of the Civil Disobedience Movement, launched with Gandhi's Dandi March in 1930. Kharaj, Jizya and Chauth are medieval taxes.
t: Link the movement to the tax it opposed.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Gandhi broke the Salt Law at Dandi on 6 April 1930 by making salt from seawater.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: C. Rajagopalachari led the salt march from Tiruchirappalli to Vedaranyam in 1930 and made salt there. Gandhi led the Dandi March.
t: Discriminate Vedaranyam from Dandi.

x: Option D is incorrect: the Champaran planters raised taxes and imposed illegal levies; they did not reduce them. The issue arose from forced indigo cultivation.
t: Check the planters' actions at Champaran.

x: Under the Tinkathia system, Champaran peasants had to grow indigo on 3 out of every 20 parts (3/20th) of their land.
t: Recall the share fixed under Tinkathia.

x: Both are true and R explains A: in 1918 the Kheda crops failed but revenue was still demanded, so the peasants launched a satyagraha for remission.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Bhag was the king's share of produce, paid by the cultivator, and was usually one-sixth in the Gupta period, following the traditional shad-bhaga.
t: Recall the standard rate of Bhag.
s: In the Gupta period, Bhag, the king's share of agricultural produce paid by the cultivator, usually amounted to:

x: I, II and IV are correct: Hiranya was a cash tax, Udrang Gupta land revenue, and Maal Mughal land revenue. III is false because Udakabhog was an irrigation tax; Uparnika was the border-land tax.
t: Discriminate Udakabhog from Uparnika.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Vishti appears in Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription and also in Gupta copper-plate inscriptions. One record does not cause the other.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Three are right: Madad-i-Mash revenue-free grants went to saints, religious institutions and mashaikhs. Mansabdars were paid through jagirs or cash, not Madad-i-Mash.
t: Separate charitable revenue-free grants from salary assignments to officers.
s:
How many of the following were recipients of Madad-i-Mash grants?
I. Saints
II. Religious institutions
III. Mashaikhs
IV. Mansabdars, in lieu of salary

x: I and II are correct: Jizya was 24 dirhams a year for incomes of 200–10,000 dirhams and 48 dirhams above 10,000. III is false because 48 dirhams applied only above 10,000.
t: Check each income slab separately.
s:
Consider the following statements regarding Aurangzeb's Jizya rates:
I. For incomes from 200 to 10,000 dirhams, the annual rate was 24 dirhams.
II. For incomes above 10,000 dirhams, the annual rate was 48 dirhams.
III. For incomes from 200 to 10,000 dirhams, the annual rate was 48 dirhams.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Gandhi led the Champaran Satyagraha of 1917 against forced indigo cultivation, his first satyagraha in India. Rajagopalachari led the Vedaranyam salt march.
t: Link the movement to its leader.

x: Bhaga was the king's share of agricultural produce, usually one-sixth. Hiranya was a cash tax, Sita revenue from crown land, and Valiam a tax on specific commodities.
t: Recall the meaning of each ancient tax term.

x: Option C is incorrect: Bali was an ancient Indian revenue, at first a voluntary offering and later a regular tax. The tax on non-Muslims was Jizya.
t: Discriminate ancient taxes from medieval Islamic taxes.

x: Uppayam was the Chola tax on salt. Irai and Vari were general Chola terms for tax, and Sardeshmukhi was a Maratha levy.
t: Recall the Chola salt tax term.

x: Valiam was a tax on specific commodities. Zakat was the religious tax on Muslims, Bhaga the share of produce, and Jagir a revenue assignment.
t: Recall the meaning of Valiam.

x: Jizya was the tax on non-Muslims under Islamic rule. Zakat was a religious tax on Muslims, Chauth a Maratha levy, and Bali an ancient Indian tax.
t: Discriminate Jizya from Zakat.

x: Sardeshmukhi was a Maratha levy of one-tenth (10%) of revenue. Chauth, the other main claim, was one-fourth.
t: Discriminate Sardeshmukhi from Chauth.

x: Iltutmish introduced the silver tanka and the copper jital. Hundi was a bill of exchange, and Dagh the branding of horses.
t: Discriminate the silver coin from the copper coin.

x: Dagh was the branding of horses, started by Alauddin Khalji to stop false musters. Iqta was a revenue assignment and Tanka a silver coin.
t: Recall the meaning of Dagh.

x: I, II and III are correct: Bhaga was the share of produce, Hiranya a cash payment and Valiam a commodity tax. IV is false because Sita was revenue from crown land; Zakat was the religious tax on Muslims.
t: Check each term separately.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Bhaga was a share of agricultural produce paid as tax.
II. Hiranya was a cash payment instead of payment in produce.
III. Valiam was a tax on specific commodities.
IV. Sita was a religious tax on Muslims.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Three are taxes: Jizya on non-Muslims, Zakat on Muslims, and the Maratha Chauth. Tanka was a silver coin introduced by Iltutmish.
t: Separate the taxes from the coin.

x: I, II and III are correct: Iqta was a Sultanate revenue assignment, Khalisa land was under direct state control, and Jagir was a Mughal assignment. IV is false because Dagh was the branding of horses; Zabt was the Mughal revenue system.
t: Check each term separately.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Iqta was a revenue assignment in the Delhi Sultanate.
II. Khalisa referred to land under direct state control.
III. Jagir was a revenue assignment to a Mansabdar or Jagirdar.
IV. Dagh was a Mughal land-revenue assessment system.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Bali was an important source of revenue in ancient India, at first a voluntary offering and later compulsory. Valiam, Hiranya and Uppayam were particular taxes.
t: Recall the ancient general revenue term.

x: Barley was the first cereal cultivated, around 8000 BC; at Mehrgarh it is the earliest evidence in the subcontinent. Rice and wheat came later, and maize arrived with the Portuguese.
t: Recall the earliest cultivated cereal.

x: Option B is incorrect: the earliest barley evidence comes from Mehrgarh, while Mahagara is known for rice and cattle pens. Lahuradeva has the oldest paddy evidence, Koldihwa was once thought oldest, and Uraiyur traded cotton.
t: Discriminate Mahagara from Mehrgarh.

x: Barley dates to c. 8000 BC, the oldest paddy comes from Lahuradeva, Uraiyur was a cotton-trade centre, and spices grew in southern India, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Link each crop to its date or place.

x: Both are true: wheat and barley were the two main food crops of the Harappans.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: All three are correct: rice was grown at Harappan sites such as Lothal and Rangpur, Harappan cotton fed textiles and trade, and Uraiyur was a cotton-trade centre.
t: Check each statement separately.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Rice was cultivated in the Harappan agricultural economy.
II. Cotton in Harappan agriculture was connected with textiles and trade.
III. Cotton trade is associated with Uraiyur.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Ibn Battuta noted that rice was sown thrice a year, maize was unknown until the Portuguese brought it, spices grew in southern India, and cotton was the Harappan textile crop, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.

Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Crop sown thrice a year, according to Ibn Battuta
(b) Crop not grown in India in the 13th–14th centuries, later brought by the Portuguese
(c) Medieval spice-growing region
(d) Harappan crop connected with textiles and trade
List-II
(i) Rice
(ii) Maize
(iii) Southern India
(iv) Cotton

x: Barley cultivation began around 8000 BC, the Harappans grew wheat and barley around 2500 BC, Ibn Battuta wrote in the 14th century, and the Portuguese brought maize in the 16th century, giving A, B, C, D.
t: Place each event in its era, from prehistoric to colonial.
s:
Arrange the following crop-related developments in chronological order:
A. Barley was first cultivated around c. 8000 BC.
B. Harappans grew wheat and barley as their main crops.
C. Ibn Battuta reported that rice could be sown thrice a year.
D. Maize was introduced into India by the Portuguese.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Firuz Tughlaq's Haqq-i-Sharb was an irrigation tax, fixed at 10% of the yield. R gives the rate, not the reason it was an irrigation tax.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Akbar's Dahsala (Zabti) used ten-year average produce and prices, the state took one-third and the cultivator kept two-thirds, and Firuz's Haqq-i-Sharb was an irrigation tax, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the shares under Akbar's revenue system.

x: The Harappans lived by agriculture, trade and crafts, the Early Vedic people by pastoralism and agriculture, the Later Vedic people more by agriculture, and Sangam society by farming, fishing, hunting, crafts and trade, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.

x: The tribes of the Godavari region of Andhra Pradesh practise Podu, a slash-and-burn form of shifting cultivation.
t: Recall the local name of shifting cultivation.

x: All four are correct: Harappans had agriculture, trade and crafts; Early Vedic people were pastoral farmers; Sangam society mixed many occupations; and medieval cultivators grew rice, wheat, sugarcane, cotton and spices.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Three are linked with crafts: the Harappans, Sangam society and artisans. Merchant guilds were linked with trade and business.
t: Check each group for craft production.

x: Uraiyur was a cotton-trade centre, Manigramam a merchant corporation, artisans engaged in craft production, and merchant guilds in trade, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Link each place or group to its activity.

x: The Harappans (c. 2500 BC) came first, then the Early Vedic people (c. 1500 BC), the Later Vedic people (c. 1000 BC) and medieval cultivators, giving C, D, A, B.
t: Arrange the groups by period.

x: Medieval cultivators grew rice, wheat, sugarcane, cotton and spices. Early Vedic people were mainly pastoral, and Godavari tribes practised shifting cultivation.
t: Link the crop list to its period.

x: Akbar abolished the Jizya in 1564 as part of his policy of religious tolerance. Firuz Tughlaq extended Jizya even to Brahmins, and Sikandar Lodi and Alauddin Khalji did not abolish it.
t: Link the year 1564 with Akbar's tolerant reforms.
s: Which of the following rulers abolished the Jizya in 1564?

x: Akbar abolished the pilgrimage tax in 1563. Shah Jahan later levied a pilgrim tax at Banaras and Allahabad.

x: Option C is incorrect: Sikandar Lodi, not Akbar, abolished the tax on grains. Zain-ul-Abidin banned cow slaughter, and Alauddin Khalji ended the privileges of the Khuts, Muqaddams and Chaudharis.
t: Link each reform to its ruler.

x: Both are true: Akbar acted against child marriage and Sati, and Shah Jahan abolished the Iranian court practice of Sijda (prostration).
t: Check each reform and its ruler separately.

x: Firuz Tughlaq's Yamuna–Hisar canal, about 150 miles long, was his longest and most important canal.
t: Recall the length of each Firuz canal.

x: Option C is incorrect: the Yamuna–Hisar canal was about 150 miles long. The 96-mile canal was the Rajabwah from the Sutlej to the Ghaggar.

t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: A is true: the Ghaggar–Firozabad canal served irrigation and public works. R is false because this canal ran from the Ghaggar; the Yamuna–Firozabad canal was a separate one.
t: Check the start point of each canal.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the Shahab or Shihab Canal belongs to Akbar's period because it was the restoration of Firuz Shah's Rajabwah carried out then.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.
